q: Across the three walk-forward folds, is FOODS_1's forecast value add improving or deteriorating?
answer: Improving, monotonically across the three folds. FOODS_1's forecast value add goes -16.3 pp (fold 1, 2013-05-05 to 2013-07-26) → -8.4 pp (fold 2, 2013-07-27 to 2013-10-24) → +4.3 pp (fold 3, 2013-10-25 to 2014-01-22), so the model only overtakes the seasonal-naive baseline in the final fold. Caveat on the mechanism: model accuracy itself is fairly flat (71.5% → 77.5% → 75.9%), while the naive baseline degrades sharply (87.8% → 85.9% → 71.6%) — the fold-3 win comes largely from the baseline getting worse, not the model getting much better. Over the full 263-day window FOODS_1 still has negative value add of -7.3 pp.

q: Which department's forecast value add deteriorates most steadily across the three backtest folds?
answer:
HOUSEHOLD_1. It is the only department whose forecast value add falls in every fold and by the largest steps: FVA of -5.0 pp in fold 1, -11.1 pp in fold 2, -12.3 pp in fold 3 (model FA 83.8% -> 77.3% -> 73.6% while the seasonal-naive stays at 88.8% / 88.4% / 85.9%). That pattern matches its worst-in-class full-window FVA of -9.4 pp, and it matters because HOUSEHOLD_1 is the second-largest department at 163,737 units.

Runners-up for a steady decline are much milder: FOODS_2 goes 0.3 -> 0.3 -> -3.2 pp (only deteriorating in the last fold). Other negative-FVA departments are not monotone — FOODS_3 runs -6.0 -> -7.7 -> -7.1 pp, HOUSEHOLD_2 -4.8 -> -13.0 -> -5.0 pp, and FOODS_1 actually improves (-16.3 -> -8.4 -> +4.3 pp). HOBBIES_2 and HOBBIES_1 stay positive throughout.

q: In December 2013, which departments actually beat the naive baseline?
answer: Scoped to the calendar window 2013-12-01 to 2013-12-31, three of the seven departments beat the seasonal-naive baseline: FOODS_1 (FA 72.0% vs naive 61.8%, FVA +10.2pp), HOBBIES_2 (59.2% vs 52.9%, +6.3pp) and HOBBIES_1 (81.5% vs 77.3%, +4.2pp). The other four lost to the baseline: HOUSEHOLD_1 badly (72.6% vs 83.8%, -11.2pp), plus HOUSEHOLD_2 (79.7% vs 80.8%, -1.1pp), FOODS_2 (78.7% vs 79.6%, -0.9pp) and FOODS_3 (80.8% vs 81.1%, -0.3pp). Note the winners are the low-volume, harder-to-predict departments, while the biggest department (FOODS_3) and the second biggest (HOUSEHOLD_1) both trailed the naive in December.

q: Which department had the largest single-day absolute forecast error anywhere in the backtest, and what happened that day?
answer: FOODS_3 on 2013-12-25 — the largest single-day absolute error in the whole backtest, 2,431.5 units. That day the store was closed (Christmas): actual sales were 0 units, but the model predicted 2,431.5. The seasonal-naive baseline made the same mistake, though smaller (1,755.0 units predicted, so 1,755.0 units of error). q: FOODS_1 loses to the naive baseline over the whole backtest — was that also true in December 2013?
answer: No — December 2013 was the opposite. Over the full 263-day backtest FOODS_1 trails the seasonal-naive baseline: 75.0% forecast accuracy vs 82.2% naive, an FVA of -7.3pp. But in the window 2013-12-01 to 2013-12-31 the model came out ahead: 72.0% accuracy vs 61.8% naive, an FVA of +10.2pp. Note what drives the flip: the model's own accuracy actually fell in December (72.0% vs 75.0% full-window), but the naive baseline degraded far more (61.8% vs 82.2%) — holiday demand breaks the repeat-last-week assumption, so the model wins by holding up better, not by forecasting better than usual.

q: Does FOODS_1 ever beat the naive baseline in any single backtest fold?
answer: Yes — in fold 3 only. FOODS_1 loses to the naive baseline in folds 1 and 2 but beats it in the final fold (2013-10-25 to 2014-01-22): FA 75.9% vs naive 71.6%, FVA +4.3pp. Fold 1 (2013-05-05 to 2013-07-26): FA 71.5% vs naive 87.8%, FVA -16.3pp. Fold 2 (2013-07-27 to 2013-10-24): FA 77.5% vs naive 85.9%, FVA -8.4pp. Note the fold-3 win comes largely from the baseline degrading (naive drops from 87.8% to 71.6%) rather than the model improving much. Over the full 263 days FOODS_1 is still negative: FA 75.0% vs naive 82.2%, FVA -7.3pp.

q: Several departments share the same worst forecast day. What date is it, and what does the data show happened?
answer:
The shared worst day is 2013-12-25 (Christmas Day). Actual sales were 0 units in every department that day — the store was closed — while both the model and the seasonal-naive baseline forecast a normal day's volume, so the entire forecast became error.

It is the single largest-error day for 5 of the 7 departments: FOODS_3 (actual 0 vs model 2,431.5 units; naive 1,755.0), HOUSEHOLD_1 (0 vs 646.9; naive 392.0), HOBBIES_1 (0 vs 481.3; naive 392.0), FOODS_2 (0 vs 382.2; naive 326.0) and HOUSEHOLD_2 (0 vs 159.9; naive 135.0). In FOODS_1 it is the second-worst day (0 vs 298.6; naive 436.0, so the naive baseline was actually worse there). HOBBIES_2 is the only department where 2013-12-25 does not appear in the top-5 error days.

Note this is a calendar closure, not a demand-model failure: neither the model nor the baseline encodes the closure, and on this day the naive error was smaller than the model error in every department except FOODS_1.

q: Is HOBBIES_2's edge over the naive baseline consistent across the three folds, and what happens to its raw accuracy over the same period?
answer:
Yes — the edge is positive and reasonably steady in all three folds, but raw accuracy deteriorates steadily.

Value add by fold: 11.7 pp (fold 1, 2013-05-05 to 2013-07-26), 8.2 pp (fold 2, 2013-07-27 to 2013-10-24), 12.3 pp (fold 3, 2013-10-25 to 2014-01-22). Full-window FVA is 10.6 pp, so the model beats seasonal-naive throughout, with fold 2 the weakest and fold 3 the strongest.

Raw accuracy falls monotonically over the same period: 72.3% → 65.8% → 60.6% (full window 65.6%). The naive baseline falls alongside it (60.6% → 57.6% → 48.3%, full window 54.9%), so the widening gap in fold 3 comes from the baseline degrading faster than the model, not from the model improving — the series is simply getting harder to forecast.

Caveat on scope: HOBBIES_2 is the smallest department in the backtest at 6,227 units over 263 days, so fold-level swings here rest on very thin volume.

q: What's HOUSEHOLD_2's value add in fold 2, and is that better or worse than its overall figure?
answer: HOUSEHOLD_2's fold-2 value add is -13.0 pp (forecast accuracy 75.4% vs naive 88.4%, 2013-07-27 to 2013-10-24). That is worse than its full-backtest value add of -7.6 pp (79.0% vs 86.6% naive). So the model loses to the seasonal-naive baseline in both views, and the gap is wider in fold 2 than over the whole 263 days.

q: Of the departments that beat the naive baseline in December 2013, which one has the highest total volume over the backtest?
answer: HOBBIES_1. Three departments beat the seasonal-naive baseline in December 2013 (2013-12-01 to 2013-12-31): HOBBIES_1 (+4.2pp FVA, 81.5% vs 77.3% naive), FOODS_1 (+10.2pp, 72.0% vs 61.8%) and HOBBIES_2 (+6.3pp, 59.2% vs 52.9%). Of those, HOBBIES_1 has the largest backtest volume at 121,662 units, ahead of FOODS_1 (86,718) and HOBBIES_2 (6,227). Note the store's biggest department, FOODS_3 (615,655 units), lost to the baseline that month (-0.3pp), as did HOUSEHOLD_1 (-11.2pp), FOODS_2 (-0.9pp) and HOUSEHOLD_2 (-1.1pp).

q: Is the model getting better over time?
answer: No — it's getting worse, not better. Pooled across all 7 departments the model averages 79.5% accuracy vs 85.2% for the seasonal-naive baseline (FVA -5.7pp), and the deterioration is visible over time in the walk-forward folds. FOODS_3 (the largest department, 615,655 units) falls from 81.8% in fold 1 to 80.4% in fold 2 to 78.2% in fold 3, with FVA staying negative throughout (-6.0, -7.7, -7.1pp). HOUSEHOLD_1 degrades more sharply: 83.8% -> 77.3% -> 73.6%, with FVA sliding from -5.0pp to -11.1pp to -12.3pp. The weekly trend tells the same story: early weeks run in the low-to-mid 80s (e.g. 86.4% week of 2013-05-20), while the last weeks sit lower (76.0% week of 2014-01-13, 68.8% week of 2014-01-20) against a naive baseline still near 87-90%. The only bright spot is HOBBIES_1, which beats naive in both fold 1 (+0.6pp) and fold 3 (+2.1pp). Note the last folds cover the holiday period, so some of the decline is seasonal difficulty rather than model drift — but the naive baseline holds up better than the model in those same weeks.

answer: Can't be answered from this backtest. The stored daily series runs 2013-05-05 to 2014-01-22, and a February 2014 window query returns no data. For reference on what is covered: pooled over the full 263-day window, forecast accuracy was 79.5% against a seasonal-naive baseline of 85.2% (FVA -5.7pp) — but that is the whole backtest, not February 2014.

q: What caused the spike in FOODS_1 sales on December 21st 2013?
answer:
I can't attribute a cause — the backtest data contains only actual, model and naive unit counts. There is nothing on promotions, prices, weather, holiday calendars or SKU mix, so any explanation would be speculation.

What the data does show for FOODS_1: 2013-12-21 was the single largest error day, with 625 actual units against a model forecast of 298.6 and a naive of 443.0 (absolute error 326.4 units). It sits inside a run of elevated December days — 471 on 12-19, 465 on 12-20, 625 on 12-21, 571 on 12-22, 535 on 12-23, 486 on 12-24 — versus a flat model level of 298.6 throughout, then 0 units on 12-25 (store closed) and 179 on 12-26. So it reads as the peak of a pre-Christmas build-up the model held flat through, but the dataset offers no driver variable to confirm why.
